## What this is

R2's depth-1 backward pass over the three anchors batch 15 deferred **by name**, plus R1's Co-1 pass. Driving gap: **GAP-002** — the determination's threshold half rested entirely on the T4–T6 regulatory stratum and no anchoring-tier source stated a maximum acceptable gradient.

Priors for all five units were committed at `589577b` **before the first query ran**. Three of the five turned out wrong, two badly, and the record says so in the search rows rather than in a footnote.

> **Read §"What happened after the first push" before reviewing the writer changes.** Two later passes found five more live defects, four of them introduced by this PR's own first commit. The sections below describe the batch; that section describes what it took to make it sound.

## The headline

**REF-01002 — Vredenburgh, Hedge, Zackowitz & Weiner 2009** (T1 clinical/high_control), *J. Architectural and Planning Research* 26(2):145–158:

> *"Results suggest that for a transit distance of up to 20 feet, a ramp should not exceed a maximum cross slope of 5% or a maximum running slope of 7%."*

The first anchoring-tier stated maximum this parameter has had, from wheelchair users' own Borg-scale perceived effort rather than a committee. Three things matter more than the number:

- **It was invisible to every DOI-keyed pass.** No DOI. It sat inside REF-00977's reference list and was reachable only by resolving a title. Two of the batch's other best candidates are also DOI-less.
- **It loosens rather than tightens.** 7 % is above the 5 % determined; the parameter direction is `lower_is_better`. The standing determination was *safe but mis-warranted* — not wrong, warranted by the wrong evidence.
- **It is held at skim grade.** The TRID record and its verbatim abstract were retrieved and persisted (HTTP 200, 50,825 bytes); **the article was not.**

Also admitted: **REF-00980** (Sanford, Story & Jones 1997 — 171 subjects across 1:8 to 1:20, declining to recommend a change; the corpus's first `confirms` edge against a code) and **REF-00979** (Chow et al. 2009 — a 4–10° inflection band, the first non-degenerate input the proxy inference has had). Two independent labs land within a rounding of each other at ~7 %; neither was designed to test the other.

## The largest effect: the determination surface is now empty

`test_db_integrity` **K02** (blocking) requires a **live** determination to account for every extraction of its parameter. This batch added five. Re-determination was attempted on a throwaway copy and **the engine crashed** — `assess_cell` reaches `provisional` on the anchored branch with `confidence=None`, and its own pydantic gate refuses it as an uncaught traceback (**GAP-019**).

What it *would* have written is its own argument against forcing it: `value_max 7.0 %`, `tier_basis T1`, `rests_on_proxy_inference 0`, `governing` and `supporting` both `None`. **A single T1 claim displaced the entire regulatory stratum** rather than composing with it — moving 5 % → 7 % and shedding the proxy marker on one skim extraction.

So **specification 8 was retired in place**. It stays readable as history at 5 % / 1:20. The cell is undetermined, which is the true state.

**And the green run now says less than it did.** `test_db_integrity` reads 74/74 — with **K01, K02 _and C10_** in its own *"PASSED HAVING EXAMINED NOTHING"* list, which grew 19 → 22. That is CLAUDE.md §5(a), produced by this batch's own remedy. Recorded as **GAP-020**, not banked. **C10 is the one that most needed naming** and the first version of this PR omitted it: *"no published cell rests on an unverified or disputed source"* examined 1 subject before this batch and 0 after — so the check that would have objected to a determination resting on REF-01002, the unverified source this batch admitted, is the check the batch silenced. Comparing 74/74 before and after compares different denominators.

## Both rankings of the three anchors were inverted

| Anchor | Batch 15 ranked | My prior | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| REF-00984 *Wheelchair skills tests* | **highest-value** | test-apparatus numbers | **0 of 38** |
| REF-00977 *Disabled-by-design* | deferred on a 403 | 0–2 relevant | 6 of 117 |
| REF-00985 *Fuzzy-logic MSD risk* | **lowest expected** | **0** | **23 of 46** |

The regularity was derivable and nobody derived it: **a paper cites the literature of its own independent variable.** **GAP-018** sets it out for prospective testing rather than adopting it on two observations. Separately: batch 15 deferred REF-00977 on a Taylor & Francis 403 — that is *full-text* inaccessibility, and backward mining never needed the full text. The Crossref deposit is free, and that generalises to every paywalled anchor.

## Owner ruling recorded on contact (rule 0)

> *"executed is 'mined'"* · *"deferred is okay so long as it runs eventually"*

Recorded in `references/project-standards.md`. It **refuses** this session's first proposed remedy — splitting `citation_mining.backward`/`.forward` into attempted/executed would be a second home for a fact `citation_mining_status` already holds (rule 5) — and confirms a deferral is not a defect. What survives: `citation_mining_completeness` counts **row presence**, so it reports deferrals as mined. What it newly opens: *"runs eventually"* is an obligation with **no mechanism** — no ageing, no backlog count, nothing that fails on an undischarged deferral.

## What happened after the first push

Two passes over the writer changes found **five more live defects, four of them introduced by this PR's own first commit.** They are listed because the pattern matters more than any one of them: every defect was found by *using* the thing, and three were in guards written to prevent the very failure they then permitted.

**Commit `daac431` — 13 code-review findings.**
- `amend-source` accepted `VERIFIED` on a row with `verification_method` NULL — the exact row `insert_source` refuses (D-0157). The comment defending the widening claimed I4 guarded it; **I4's subject is `verification_status='VERIFIED' AND verification_method IS NOT NULL`, so a NULL-method row is invisible to it.** A guard cited as protection that cannot see the row.
- No vocabulary gate at all: `verrified` stored cleanly and silently dropped the row out of every I-check.
- `log-mining`'s deferral discharge cleared `deferred_reason` **regardless of direction** — one column, two directions — so a backward pass discharged REF-00989's *forward* deferral and marked the source mined, erasing exactly the owed work the ruling above depends on.
- `notes` was replaced rather than merged, destroying prior passes' records; the "cannot assert both" refusal read only argv; a valid ref against the wrong slug raised a raw `IntegrityError`.

**Commit `5dbc20d` — four cleanup agents (reuse / simplification / efficiency / altitude).** Two findings were live defects, both mine:
- **`is_mined` reported ten fully-mined anchors as unmined.** `executed` collapsed NULL to False. A `citation_mining` row's `global_ref_id` may name a `source_locators` *lead* — migration 067 dropped that FK deliberately, *"a ref_id is an identity that SPANS two tables"*. **10 of 23 live rows**, every one fully mined. The skill step added in the same diff says *"if `executed` is false → mine the missing direction(s)"*, so it commanded re-mining finished work — verbatim the RAP-F61/F69/F70 failure that same skill file records.
- **The regression guard keyed on `notes` being non-empty, and was wrong both ways.** A `--connections` pass sets `status='mined'` and writes no notes, so the guard stayed silent on the skill's own documented happy path; and it fired on lead anchors that have no status to regress.

Both now go through **one** `mining_executed()` derivation returning `true`/`false`/`null`, with `null` explicitly not `false`. Also: `amend_source` called `connect(True)` — positional `dry_run=True`, **not** `readonly=True` — so it opened the canonical blob read-write and dbcore's rule-3 guard refused it, making the D-0157 invariant unreachable on the one database it most needed to hold for. Two hand-typed vocabularies replaced with `check_vocab` and an `ENUM_GUARDS` import (rule 8); a duplicate SELECT that ran *after* the write; dead `status_explicit` state; unreachable `or carried`; and the hard-coded `10/10, 100.0%` / `3 of 13` figures removed from a skill file — rule 7a, sitting inside the paragraph explaining the figure is wrong.

**Rule 4 was broken and then swept.** The first commit changed the writer contract and swept no callers; `citation-miner` and `research-log-manager` both still directed operators to `deferred_reason` for a pass that ran — the false deferral the change exists to eliminate.

**Deliberately skipped**, recorded rather than argued with: changing `citation_mining_completeness` to read status rather than row presence (correct, but **GAP-022 says it must land with the missing "runs eventually" measure so the percentage does not move silently** — landing half is what that gap warns against), and re-graining `citation_mining` per direction (collides with GAP-015, unruled).

## Gates

- `research_batch_dod --session <id>` → **COMPLIANT**, all 19 rules
- `citation_mining_completeness --session <id>.md` → **CLEAN**, `EXAMINED: 3`
- `test_db_integrity` → **74/74** (see the §5(a) caveat above)
- `run_checks --changed-from origin/main` → **PASS**, no blocking failures
- `run_checks --selftest` → **PASS**; baseline ratchets down only

`data/guidebook.db` is byte-unchanged by both follow-up commits, so no compensating migration is owed for either.

The blocking battery was run **after** the first migration was applied — the exact error batch 13's attestation warned the next session about. Three failures followed against a 74/74 baseline. Recoverable only because nothing was committed: canonical restored, the uncommitted migration deleted, corrections made in the scratch, one clean migration re-emitted. Logged as a deviation.

## Owed

1. **GAP-016 (P1)** — read Vredenburgh in full. Four things the abstract does not answer are named on the gap.
2. **GAP-019 / GAP-020 (P1)** — the engine cannot emit an anchored `provisional` cell, and behind it a single T1 claim displacing the regulatory stratum. Needs a ruling, not a defect fix.
3. **GAP-022 (P1)** — make the completeness check read status not presence, and build the missing measure for "runs eventually", landing both together.
4. REF-01002's backward set; candidate 96 (Gagnon 2014, open access) as a third-lab test of the inflection band.

## Reviewer's strongest line, stated rather than buried

The batch's net effect on the guidebook is that it **removed the only live determination the project had**. Before it, a reader asking for a ramp gradient got 5 %, provisional, marked a proxy; after it they get nothing — and the source that caused the removal is one nobody has read past its abstract, from an index whose publisher field for that same record is demonstrably wrong. Every instrument invoked is real and correctly used, and K02 forced the choice while the engine removed the alternative. The honest reading is that **the project's ability to hold a determination while evidence accumulates is what actually failed here**, and this batch found it by tripping over it rather than by auditing for it.

A second line a reviewer is entitled to press: **the writer changes needed three passes to become sound**, and the defects found in passes two and three were in guards written during pass one to prevent the exact failures they then permitted. The record above is complete rather than flattering, but "found by using it" is not the same as "designed correctly", and this diff is the former.

{"number":152,"title":"Research batch 16 — backward mining of the three deferred anchors; the first anchoring-tier ramp-gradient maximum, and an empty determination surface","body":"## What this is

R2's depth-1 backward pass over the three anchors batch 15 deferred **by name**, plus R1's Co-1 pass. Driving gap: **GAP-002** — the determination's threshold half rested entirely on the T4–T6 regulatory stratum and no anchoring-tier source stated a maximum acceptable gradient.

Priors for all five units were committed at `589577b` **before the first query ran**. Three of the five turned out wrong, two badly, and the record says so in the search rows rather than in a footnote.

> **Read §"What happened after the first push" before reviewing the writer changes.** Two later passes found five more live defects, four of them introduced by this PR's own first commit. The sections below describe the batch; that section describes what it took to make it sound.

## The headline

**REF-01002 — Vredenburgh, Hedge, Zackowitz & Weiner 2009** (T1 clinical/high_control), *J. Architectural and Planning Research* 26(2):145–158:

> *"Results suggest that for a transit distance of up to 20 feet, a ramp should not exceed a maximum cross slope of 5% or a maximum running slope of 7%."*

The first anchoring-tier stated maximum this parameter has had, from wheelchair users' own Borg-scale perceived effort rather than a committee. Three things matter more than the number:

- **It was invisible to every DOI-keyed pass.** No DOI. It sat inside REF-00977's reference list and was reachable only by resolving a title. Two of the batch's other best candidates are also DOI-less.
- **It loosens rather than tightens.** 7 % is above the 5 % determined; the parameter direction is `lower_is_better`. The standing determination was *safe but mis-warranted* — not wrong, warranted by the wrong evidence.
- **It is held at skim grade.** The TRID record and its verbatim abstract were retrieved and persisted (HTTP 200, 50,825 bytes); **the article was not.**

Also admitted: **REF-00980** (Sanford, Story & Jones 1997 — 171 subjects across 1:8 to 1:20, declining to recommend a change; the corpus's first `confirms` edge against a code) and **REF-00979** (Chow et al. 2009 — a 4–10° inflection band, the first non-degenerate input the proxy inference has had). Two independent labs land within a rounding of each other at ~7 %; neither was designed to test the other.

## The largest effect: the determination surface is now empty

`test_db_integrity` **K02** (blocking) requires a **live** determination to account for every extraction of its parameter. This batch added five. Re-determination was attempted on a throwaway copy and **the engine crashed** — `assess_cell` reaches `provisional` on the anchored branch with `confidence=None`, and its own pydantic gate refuses it as an uncaught traceback (**GAP-019**).

What it *would* have written is its own argument against forcing it: `value_max 7.0 %`, `tier_basis T1`, `rests_on_proxy_inference 0`, `governing` and `supporting` both `None`. **A single T1 claim displaced the entire regulatory stratum** rather than composing with it — moving 5 % → 7 % and shedding the proxy marker on one skim extraction.

So **specification 8 was retired in place**. It stays readable as history at 5 % / 1:20. The cell is undetermined, which is the true state.

**And the green run now says less than it did.** `test_db_integrity` reads 74/74 — with **K01, K02 _and C10_** in its own *"PASSED HAVING EXAMINED NOTHING"* list, which grew 19 → 22. That is CLAUDE.md §5(a), produced by this batch's own remedy. Recorded as **GAP-020**, not banked. **C10 is the one that most needed naming** and the first version of this PR omitted it: *"no published cell rests on an unverified or disputed source"* examined 1 subject before this batch and 0 after — so the check that would have objected to a determination resting on REF-01002, the unverified source this batch admitted, is the check the batch silenced. Comparing 74/74 before and after compares different denominators.

## Both rankings of the three anchors were inverted

| Anchor | Batch 15 ranked | My prior | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| REF-00984 *Wheelchair skills tests* | **highest-value** | test-apparatus numbers | **0 of 38** |
| REF-00977 *Disabled-by-design* | deferred on a 403 | 0–2 relevant | 6 of 117 |
| REF-00985 *Fuzzy-logic MSD risk* | **lowest expected** | **0** | **23 of 46** |

The regularity was derivable and nobody derived it: **a paper cites the literature of its own independent variable.** **GAP-018** sets it out for prospective testing rather than adopting it on two observations. Separately: batch 15 deferred REF-00977 on a Taylor & Francis 403 — that is *full-text* inaccessibility, and backward mining never needed the full text. The Crossref deposit is free, and that generalises to every paywalled anchor.

## Owner ruling recorded on contact (rule 0)

> *"executed is 'mined'"* · *"deferred is okay so long as it runs eventually"*

Recorded in `references/project-standards.md`. It **refuses** this session's first proposed remedy — splitting `citation_mining.backward`/`.forward` into attempted/executed would be a second home for a fact `citation_mining_status` already holds (rule 5) — and confirms a deferral is not a defect. What survives: `citation_mining_completeness` counts **row presence**, so it reports deferrals as mined. What it newly opens: *"runs eventually"* is an obligation with **no mechanism** — no ageing, no backlog count, nothing that fails on an undischarged deferral.

## What happened after the first push

Two passes over the writer changes found **five more live defects, four of them introduced by this PR's own first commit.** They are listed because the pattern matters more than any one of them: every defect was found by *using* the thing, and three were in guards written to prevent the very failure they then permitted.

**Commit `daac431` — 13 code-review findings.**
- `amend-source` accepted `VERIFIED` on a row with `verification_method` NULL — the exact row `insert_source` refuses (D-0157). The comment defending the widening claimed I4 guarded it; **I4's subject is `verification_status='VERIFIED' AND verification_method IS NOT NULL`, so a NULL-method row is invisible to it.** A guard cited as protection that cannot see the row.
- No vocabulary gate at all: `verrified` stored cleanly and silently dropped the row out of every I-check.
- `log-mining`'s deferral discharge cleared `deferred_reason` **regardless of direction** — one column, two directions — so a backward pass discharged REF-00989's *forward* deferral and marked the source mined, erasing exactly the owed work the ruling above depends on.
- `notes` was replaced rather than merged, destroying prior passes' records; the "cannot assert both" refusal read only argv; a valid ref against the wrong slug raised a raw `IntegrityError`.

**Commit `5dbc20d` — four cleanup agents (reuse / simplification / efficiency / altitude).** Two findings were live defects, both mine:
- **`is_mined` reported ten fully-mined anchors as unmined.** `executed` collapsed NULL to False. A `citation_mining` row's `global_ref_id` may name a `source_locators` *lead* — migration 067 dropped that FK deliberately, *"a ref_id is an identity that SPANS two tables"*. **10 of 23 live rows**, every one fully mined. The skill step added in the same diff says *"if `executed` is false → mine the missing direction(s)"*, so it commanded re-mining finished work — verbatim the RAP-F61/F69/F70 failure that same skill file records.
- **The regression guard keyed on `notes` being non-empty, and was wrong both ways.** A `--connections` pass sets `status='mined'` and writes no notes, so the guard stayed silent on the skill's own documented happy path; and it fired on lead anchors that have no status to regress.

# MISLINKED / UNDER-CONSERVATIVE and FDR delta-classification CONTRADICTS "force the
    # affected cell to `provisional` -- never `stated` -- until resolved." That is a CAP,
    # not a downgrade ladder: a gate never lifts a `pending` cell up to provisional, and
    # never pushes a provisional cell lower. The ladder-inversion guard is upstream, in
    # derivation_handshake(), which marks a gate weaker than the cell's best anchor
    # `binds: False` rather than dropping it -- so a grey-tier CONTRADICTS cannot pin a
    # T1-anchored cell, and a reader can still see the gate existed and why it did not bite.
    #
    # THE GATE IS NOT COPIED ONTO THE DETERMINATION, and that is rule 5 rather than an
    # omission. A gate row is addressed by (parameter_id, identity_code) and reachable
    # through `v_open_determination_gates`; writing its id into `specifications` as well
    # would build the second home that a parity check can only make permanent. What the
    # row carries is the EFFECT -- a cell with anchors in `tier_basis` sitting at
    # `provisional` -- and `derivation_handshake_integrity` is what holds the two in step.

input.command:
S=scratchpad/session_2026-09-18-research-batch-16-backward-mining-t2-anchors && SESS=session_2026-09-18-research-batch-16-backward-mining-t2-anchors && G="$S/walk2.db"
for g in GAP-019 GAP-010; do :; done
GUIDEBOOK_DB_PATH="$G" python3 scripts/db.py close-gap --gap-id GAP-019 --status CLOSED-FIXED --session "$SESS"
GUIDEBOOK_DB_PATH="$G" python3 scripts/db.py add-gap --category RP --priority P1 --session "$SESS" \
 --description 'BATCH 17 MINING ASSIGNMENT — owner instruction 2026-09-18, answering GAP-022: "then assign the mining for the next batch". THE MECHANISM FOR "runs eventually" IS ASSIGNMENT, NOT AN AGEING METRIC. GAP-022 named the missing half of the 2026-09-18 ruling (deferred is okay so long as it runs eventually) and proposed building an age or backlog measure. The owner answered by assigning the work instead, which is the cheaper and more honest instrument: a deferral runs because a batch is told to run it, not because a counter goes red. DERIVE THE BACKLOG, NEVER QUOTE IT -- select slug, global_ref_id, deferred_reason from citation_mining where deferred_reason is not null; measured 2026-09-18 at ten rows, all on accessible-circulation-geometry. BATCH 17 TAKES THESE, IN THIS ORDER, AND THE ORDER IS REASONED. (1) REF-01002 backward -- the highest-value target on the slug by its own framing, a 2009 study saying design recommendations for either the running slope or the cross slope requirements are based on limited empirical research, so it cites whatever empirical work existed. BLOCKED BEHIND GAP-016: no DOI, therefore no Crossref deposit, so its reference list can only come from the article, which GAP-016 must obtain anyway to settle C10. Reading it discharges both. (2) REF-00979 backward -- ranks second on the GAP-018 predictor (a paper cites the literature of its own independent variable; Chow et al. measure propulsion across a slope series), and mining it is therefore also a PROSPECTIVE TEST of that predictor, with the prediction already recorded in its deferral note before the pass. (3) REF-00980 backward -- a 1997 paper cites pre-1997 work, and the pre-1997 ramp-slope literature is exactly what REF-01002 abstract calls limited; expected yield modest, stated in advance. (4) REF-00983 and REF-00986 backward -- batch 08 deferrals, the oldest in the register, and REF-00986 own extraction is graded absent so its references are unlikely to be gradient-bearing; both cheap. (5) REF-00999, REF-01000, REF-01001 backward -- T3, so R2 depth-2-3 obligation over CONFIRMED T1-T2 anchors reaches them only secondarily; take them only if capacity remains. (6) REF-00989 and REF-00993 FORWARD -- both Japanese-language, no DOI, absent from every citation index, so the forward graph does not reach them. THESE TWO ARE NOT A MINING PASS AND MUST NOT BE DRESSED AS ONE: the tractable equivalent is a Japanese-language site search for organisations quoting the same framing, which is a SEARCH and is recorded as owed. WHAT DISCHARGE REQUIRES: a pass that runs clears its deferral only with --discharge-deferral, which asserts the standing deferral belongs to the direction just run; without it the deferral stands and log-mining prints deferral_still_standing. Batch 17 closes this gap by emptying the backlog or by re-deferring with fresh reasons -- never by silence.'
echo "=== assignment recorded ==="

GAP-022 named the missing half of the 2026-09-18 ruling (deferred is okay so long as it runs eventually) and proposed building an age or backlog measure. The owner answered by assigning the work instead, which is the cheaper and more honest instrument: a deferral runs because a batch is told to run it, not because a counter goes red. DERIVE THE BACKLOG, NEVER QUOTE IT -- select slug, global_ref_id, deferred_reason from citation_mining where deferred_reason is not null; measured 2026-09-18 at ten rows, all on accessible-circulation-geometry. BATCH 17 TAKES THESE, IN THIS ORDER, AND THE ORDER IS REASONED. (1) REF-01002 backward -- the highest-value target on the slug by its own framing, a 2009 study saying design recommendations for either the running slope or the cross slope requirements are based on limited empirical research, so it cites whatever empirical work existed. BLOCKED BEHIND GAP-016: no DOI, therefore no Crossref deposit, so its reference list can only come from the article, which GAP-016 must obtain anyway to settle C10. Reading it discharges both. (2) REF-00979 backward -- ranks second on the GAP-018 predictor (a paper cites the literature of its own independent variable; Chow et al. measure propulsion across a slope series), and mining it is therefore also a PROSPECTIVE TEST of that predictor, with the prediction already recorded in its deferral note before the pass. (3) REF-00980 backward -- a 1997 paper cites pre-1997 work, and the pre-1997 ramp-slope literature is exactly what REF-01002 abstract calls limited; expected yield modest, stated in advance. (4) REF-00983 and REF-00986 backward -- batch 08 deferrals, the oldest in the register, and REF-00986 own extraction is graded absent so its references are unlikely to be gradient-bearing; both cheap. (5) REF-00999, REF-01000, REF-01001 backward -- T3, so R2 depth-2-3 obligation over CONFIRMED T1-T2 anchors reaches them only secondarily; take them only if capacity remains. (6) REF-00989 and REF-00993 FORWARD -- both Japanese-language, no DOI, absent from every citation index, so the forward graph does not reach them. THESE TWO ARE NOT A MINING PASS AND MUST NOT BE DRESSED AS ONE: the tractable equivalent is a Japanese-language site search for organisations quoting the same framing, which is a SEARCH and is recorded as owed. WHAT DISCHARGE REQUIRES: a pass that runs clears its deferral only with --discharge-deferral, which asserts the standing deferral belongs to the direction just run; without it the deferral stands and log-mining prints deferral_still_standing. Batch 17 closes this gap by emptying the backlog or by re-deferring with fresh reasons -- never by silence.', '2026-09-18 21:04', 'session_2026-09-18-research-batch-16-backward-mining-t2-anchors', '2026-09-18 21:04', 'session_2026-09-18-research-batch-16-backward-mining-t2-anchors', NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL);

Both done, pushed as `1825003` (commit message via `-F` this time, so the backticks survived).

## GAP-019 — resolved, and it was never doctrine

The engine's **gate cap** (`state == "stated"` + any binding gate → `provisional`) downgraded the cell **without supplying the confidence flag `provisional` requires**, so the pydantic model refused it and nothing was written. `determination_gates` held **zero rows** until this batch raised gate 1 — so that branch had never executed in the engine's life. **The crash was created by the first gate ever raised, which was mine**, and I then escalated it to you as a pre-existing doctrinal gap needing a ruling. That was the worse error of the two. The fix is descriptive: `present` is the anchoring basis the cell already has, `absent` names the gate.

## A retraction you should see

GAP-019 also claimed **a single T1 claim displaced the entire regulatory stratum**, citing `governing` and `supporting` both `None`. **That is false.** I printed `det.get("governing")`; the key is `governing_refs`, and it reads `["REF-01002"]` correctly. The regulatory sources leaving the governing set once an anchor exists is **the ratified ladder working** — T4–T6 walled off from full-strength anchoring — not a defect.

The claim was dramatic, it flattered this batch's caution, and it reached a gap, the session record, the attestation and the PR body before anyone re-derived it. All four corrected; GAP-023 carries it.

## GAP-020 — answered mechanically, not closed

With the engine fixed I rehearsed the re-determination on a throwaway copy. It succeeds: `provisional`, 7 %, `tier_basis T1`, governed by REF-01002, cap recorded in the flag. K01 and K02 come back to one subject each.

**Then C10 fails** — *"no published cell rests on an unverified or disputed source"* — because REF-01002 is `UNVERIFIED`, the grade I4 forced. 73/74 on the rehearsal.

So your own blocking check refuses the re-determination, for exactly the reason the batch refused it by hand. That converts my judgement call into a measurement. The empty surface is correct until GAP-016 closes, and the path out is fully specified: read the full text → verify → re-determine → C10 passes → resolve gate 1. Nothing was applied; canonical carries the gap rows only.

## GAP-022 — closed by assignment

Taking your instruction as the mechanism: a deferral runs because a batch is told to run it, not because a counter goes red. GAP-025 assigns **all ten** undischarged deferrals to batch 17 in a reasoned order — REF-01002 first (highest-value by its own framing, and blocked behind GAP-016, which must read it anyway, so one read discharges both); REF-00979 second **as a prospective test of GAP-018's predictor**, with the prediction recorded in its deferral note before the pass; then the batch-08 deferrals; then the T3 tail. The two Japanese-language *forward* deferrals are flagged as **not a mining pass and not to be dressed as one** — no citation index reaches them, so the honest equivalent is a search.

# Batch 17 — prior expectations, written BEFORE execution

Session: `session_2026-09-18-research-batch-17-vredenburgh-full-read-and-mining`
Parameter: 3 (`ramp gradient`, TERM-001) × MOB, slug `accessible-circulation-geometry`.
Live state: **no determination** — spec 8 retired in place; determination gate 1 OPEN.

Assignment: **GAP-025**, the batch-17 mining order the owner set when closing GAP-022
("then assign the mining for the next batch"). Its first item is blocked behind **GAP-016**,
and one read discharges both.

DR-2026-05-09: a prior recorded after seeing results is a rationalisation.

---

## A1 — Obtain and read REF-01002 in full (GAP-016)

Vredenburgh, Hedge, Zackowitz & Weiner 2009, *J. Architectural and Planning Research*
26(2):145–158. **No DOI.** Held at skim grade on a TRID record.

**Prior on retrievability.** JAPR is a small independent journal (Locke Science) with no
DOI registration and no open archive I expect to resolve. Routes, in order: JSTOR (JAPR is
indexed there), a university repository copy by author, ResearchGate/Academia (both
surfaced in batch 16's title resolution), and the authors' own pages — Hedge was Cornell
DEA, Vredenburgh runs a human-factors consultancy that publishes its papers. **I expect
retrieval to be the hard part of this batch and I put it below even odds.** If it fails,
that is a recorded null and the figure stays where it is; it is not licence to promote the
extraction.

**Priors on the four questions GAP-016 names.**
1. *Participant count.* Expect **20–40**, typical of a within-subject perception study with
   comparative judgements. Expect both manual and powered users, unevenly split.
2. *Slope set tested.* **This is the one that matters.** I expect a factorial of running
   slope × cross slope at discrete levels, and I expect 7 % to be **at or near the top of
   the tested range** — which would make "should not exceed 7 %" a statement about where
   perceived effort degraded within what was tested, not an unbounded recommendation.
   **If so, the extraction's `claim_type=numerical` with `comparator='<='` is right but its
   reading needs narrowing, and I should say so rather than bank the figure.**
3. *The 20-foot bound.* Expect it is the **apparatus length**, not a tested variable — i.e.
   a constraint of the ramp they built, reported as a scope limit. If that is so, extraction
   44 (`condition`, 20 ft) is correctly filed but its `claim_type=numerical` overstates: it
   would be an apparatus fact, not a finding.
4. *Co-1.* **Expect NOT Co-1.** Four named authors, two of them human-factors academics and
   one a consultancy principal; no disabled people's organisation in the byline. Expect
   participants recruited as subjects. Under D-0178 that is participation, not
   co-production — the same answer GAP-014 reached for REF-01001. **I am recording this
   expectation precisely because a Co-1 finding would be convenient**: it would make the
   source co-primary with T1 and strengthen the cell I want to re-determine.

## A2 — Verification, and what it unblocks

If the full text is obtained, REF-01002's `verification_status` moves UNVERIFIED →
VERIFIED with `verification_method=direct-render`, and **C10 stops refusing the
re-determination**. Then: promote extraction 45 from skim/preliminary, re-determine
parameter 3 × MOB, resolve gate 1.

**Prior on the re-determination.** Rehearsed in batch 16 on a throwaway: `provisional`,
`value_max 7.0 %`, `tier_basis T1`, governed by REF-01002. I expect the same, and I expect
it to remain **`provisional` rather than `stated`** while gate 1 is open — the cap is what
makes that so, and resolving the gate is a separate act that should follow the read, not
accompany it.

## M1 — REF-01002 backward (GAP-025 item 1)

**Prior.** Its own abstract says design recommendations "are based on limited empirical
research", so I expect a **short** relevant reference list — perhaps 20–40 entries, of which
**2–5** bear on slope. No DOI means no Crossref deposit: the list must come from the article,
so this is blocked behind A1 and dies with it.

## M2 — REF-00979 backward (GAP-025 item 2) — A PRE-REGISTERED TEST

Chow et al. 2009. Its deferral note already carries the prediction, written before this
batch: under GAP-018's predictor — *a paper cites the literature of its own independent
variable* — Chow measures propulsion across a slope series, so it should cite the
propulsion-on-slopes literature.

**Quantified so the test can fail:** I predict **≥ 8 of its references** match the
ramp/slope/gradient screen. Batch 16's observed rates were 23/46 (REF-00985, a slope-series
biomechanics paper) against 0/38 (REF-00984, an instrument review). If Chow returns < 5,
the predictor is weakened and GAP-018 must record that rather than quietly dropping it.

## M3 — REF-00980 backward (GAP-025 item 3)

Sanford 1997. **Prior: low yield, 0–2 relevant.** A 1997 paper cites pre-1997 work, and
pre-1997 ramp-slope empirical literature is exactly what REF-01002 calls limited. Run
because GAP-025 assigns it and a null on a named anchor is a completed unit of work.

## S1 — Co-1 pass (R1, runs FIRST regardless)

Batches 09–12 covered EN/DE/FR/NL/ES/JA; batch 16 added HR and SV, both well-formed zero
yields. **Prior: another generic pass re-finds nothing.** The untried angle with real
prospect is a DPO that publishes an access-audit *standard* rather than advocacy — expect
low yield, and expect any hit to be T5/T6 regulatory restatement rather than Co-1, which is
what the SV pass found. Possibility of zero is real and would be the third consecutive one.

---

## What would falsify this batch's premise

If the full text shows 7 % is the highest slope **tested** rather than a recommendation,
then the "first anchoring-tier stated maximum" framing batch 16 built — and put in a PR
title — is **wrong**, and extraction 45 must be re-described under R15 rather than promoted.
I think this is a live possibility, around one in three, and it is the outcome I am least
inclined to see. Recording it here so the read is a test.

## Named dissenter

The reading against this batch: it spends its effort on retrieving one paywalled 2009 paper
with no DOI, and if retrieval fails it has produced a null, two backward passes, and nothing
else. A defender would say the read is what unblocks the determination, C10 and gate 1
together — which is true, and is also exactly what a batch would say to justify a single
expensive bet.
EOF

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about Vredenburgh Associates' publications:

Vredenburgh, A. G., A. Hedge, I. B. Zackowitz, and J. M. Welner published "Evaluation of Wheelchair Users' Perceived Sidewalk and Ramp Slope: Effort and Accessibility" in 2009 in the Journal of Architectural and Planning Research.

This study evaluated the degree to which users of manual and motorized wheelchairs could perceive differences in the running slope or in the cross slope of ramps and in the perceived effort required to negotiate these ramps. 

Participants traversed two adjoining ramps with different combinations of running slope and cross slope and made comparative judgments of slope differences. Results suggest that for a transit distance up to 6 m (20 ft.), a ramp should not exceed a maximum cross slope of 5% or a maximum running slope of 7%.

This publication is a key human factors study related to wheelchair accessibility and the perception of slope in ramps and sidewalks.

content.text:
Found 10 papers, showing top 10.

[1] [Evaluation of wheelchair users' perceived sidewalk and ramp slope: effort and accessibility](https://consensus.app/papers/details/cc57ca29a6545da7849a58c6ab9f9905/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (Alison G. Vredenburgh et al., 2009, 10 citations, Journal of Architectural and Planning Research)
  The use of ramps to improve building accessibility for wheelchair users is required by the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Fair Housing Act, and various building codes, all of which specify requirements for ramp design, including their maximum running slope and cross slope. Design recommendations for either the running slope or the cross slope requirements are based on limited empirical research. This study evaluated the degree to which users of manual and motorized wheelchairs could perceive differences in the running slope or in the cross slope of ramps and in the perceived effort (Borg scale) required to negotiate these ramps. Participants traversed two adjoining ramps with different combinations of running slope and cross slope and made comparative judgments of slope differences. Results suggest that for a transit distance up to 6 m (20 ft), a ramp should not exceed a maximum cross slope of 5% or a maximum running slope of 7%.

[2] [Analysis of the effect of path cross slope on manual wheelchair propulsion](https://consensus.app/papers/details/efb3625e761f590c8afb69666d13dc94/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (C. Flemmer et al., 2026, 1 citations, Disability and Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology)
  Purpose: Asymmetrical arm use is needed to propel a manual wheelchair on a straight trajectory when the path has cross slope. Beyond being tiring and inefficient, little is known about the implications of cross slope.

Method: Simple mechanics is used to analyse the forces acting on the front casters of a wheelchair on a compound slope. This is used to determine how varying cross slope affects the user's propulsion.

Results: Analysis shows that the effect of cross slope on compound slopes is relatively small, slightly decreasing the equivalent running slope that can be achieved for the same user effort. The greater the cross slope, the greater the effect. Shifting user weight towards the rear wheels minimises the cross slope impact. Cross slope has a significant effect on paths with small running slope. For specific wheelchair-user conditions, the critical cross slope at zero running slope for which the wheelchair user must propel using only the downslope pushrim was estimated to be 3%. Further increase in cross slope necessitates braking on the upslope pushrim and imposes large propulsion effort on the downslope pushrim, which is fatiguing over long distances.

Conclusion: This work contributes insights into cross slope and a simple method for quantifying the magnitude of its effect on wheelchair users. Better regulation of cross slope would improve the accessibility of outdoor paths for manual wheelchairs users.

[3] [Quantifying cardiorespiratory responses resulting from speed and slope increments during motorized treadmill propulsion among manual wheelchair users.](https://consensus.app/papers/details/425f8fdf3e21551295c5bbd388e4b44f/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (C. Gauthier et al., 2017, 9 citations, Annals of physical and rehabilitation medicine)
  Background: Cardiorespiratory fitness assessment and training among manual wheelchair (MW) users are predominantly done with an arm-crank ergometer. However, arm-crank ergometer biomechanics differ substantially from MW propulsion biomechanics. This study aimed to quantify cardiorespiratory responses resulting from speed and slope increments during MW propulsion on a motorized treadmill and to calculate a predictive equation based on speed and slope for estimating peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) in MW users.

Methods: In total, 17 long-term MW users completed 12 MW propulsion periods (PP), each lasting 2min, on a motorized treadmill, in a random order. Each PP was separated by a 2-min rest. PPs were characterized by a combination of 3 speeds (0.6, 0.8 and 1.0m/s) and 4 slopes (0°, 2.7°, 3.6° and 4.8°). Six key cardiorespiratory outcome measures (VO2, heart rate, respiratory rate, minute ventilation and tidal volume) were recorded by using a gas-exchange analysis system. Rate of perceived exertion (RPE) was measured by using the modified 10-point Borg scale after each PP.

Results: For the 14 participants who completed the test, cardiorespiratory responses increased in response to speed and/or slope increments, except those recorded between the 3.6o and 4.8o slope, for which most outcome measures were comparable. The RPE was positively associated with cardiorespiratory response (rs≥0.85). A VO2 predictive equation (R2=99.7%) based on speed and slope for each PP was computed. This equation informed the development of a future testing protocol to linearly increase VO2 via 1-min stages during treadmill MW propulsion.

Conclusions: Increasing speed and slope while propelling a MW on a motorized treadmill increases cardiorespiratory response along with RPE. RPE can be used to easily and accurately monitor cardiorespiratory responses during MW exercise. The VO2 can be predicted to some extent by speed and slope during MW propulsion. A testing protocol is proposed to assess cardiorespiratory fitness during motorized MW propulsion.

Copyright © 2017 Elsevier Masson SAS. All rights reserved.

[4] [Effect of Manual Wheelchair Type on Mobility Performance, Cardiorespiratory Responses, and Perceived Exertion](https://consensus.app/papers/details/bafcccab8d6f542eb746c8ffa4554b45/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (G. da Silva Bertolaccini et al., 2022, 14 citations, Rehabilitation Research and Practice)
  This study is aimed at comparing the design and configuration of the most commonly used manual wheelchair models through cardiorespiratory responses, perceived exertion, and mobility performance using two different manual wheelchairs, during mobility tasks. A within-group 2 × 3 × 2 controlled experiment was designed with three independent and four dependent variables. The independent variables included wheelchairs, with the levels active wheelchair with a rigid frame and passive wheelchair with foldable frame; conditions with the levels straight line, slalom, and agility; and speed with levels comfortable and fast. Dependent variables included oxygen uptake (VO2), distance travelled, speed, and perceived exertion. Results show that the active wheelchair yielded more beneficial characteristics although only the effect of wheelchair type on VO2 efficiency (oxygen uptake per meter travelled) was statistically significant with a large effect size (F(1, 14) = 118.298, p < 0.001, η 2 = 0.541). The better VO2 efficiency was achieved with the active wheelchair under all tested conditions. The effect of wheelchair type on Borg scores was also statistically significant, although with a small effect size (F(1, 14) = 10.340, p = 0.006, η 2 = 0.119); thus, active wheelchair use had lower Borg scores under all trials and was considered less exhausting than the passive wheelchair. In summary, use of the active wheelchair resulted in the users expending less energy per meter travelled and at the same time experiencing less fatigue. This may benefit overall wheelchair mobility and possibly reduce health complications.

Copyright © 2022 Guilherme da Silva Bertolaccini et al.

[5] [Manual wheelchair biomechanics while overcoming various environmental barriers: A systematic review](https://consensus.app/papers/details/94c878edc4775f4b871d86112fc27b1d/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (Théo Rouvier et al., 2022, 14 citations, PLoS ONE)
  During manual wheelchair (MWC) locomotion, the user's upper limbs are subject to heavy stresses and fatigue because the upper body is permanently engaged to propel the MWC. These stresses and fatigue vary according to the environmental barriers encountered outdoors along a given path. This study aimed at conducting a systematic review of the literature assessing the biomechanics of MWC users crossing various situations, which represent physical environmental barriers. Through a systematic search on PubMed, 34 articles were selected and classified according to the investigated environmental barriers: slope; cross-slope; curb; and ground type. For each barrier, biomechanical parameters were divided into four categories: spatiotemporal parameters; kinematics; kinetics; and muscle activity. All results from the different studies were gathered, including numerical data, and assessed with respect to the methodology used in each study. This review sheds light on the fact that certain situations (cross-slopes and curbs) or parameters (kinematics) have scarcely been studied, and that a wider set of situations should be studied. Five recommendations were made at the end of this review process to standardize the procedure when reporting materials, methods, and results for the study of biomechanics of any environmental barrier encountered in MWC locomotion: (i) effectively reporting barriers' lengths, grades, or heights; (ii) striving for standardization or a report of the approach conditions of the barrier, such as velocity, especially on curbs; (iii) reporting the configuration of the used MWC, and if it was fitted to the subject's morphology; (iv) reporting rotation sequences for the expression of moments and kinematics, and when used, the definition of the musculoskeletal model; lastly (v) when possible, reporting measurement uncertainties and model reconstruction errors.

[6] [Impact of Running Slope and Cross Slope on the Difficulty Level of Outdoor Pathways](https://consensus.app/papers/details/95a5024e8d8e50e687504f81f8dc7ed8/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (P. Longmuir et al., 2003, 16 citations, Environment and Behavior)
  This pilot study examined proposed accessibility guidelines for running slope and cross slope and the perceived difficulty ratings of individuals with mobility limitations. Participants were 23 men and women, 23 to 67 years, with vision or mobility limitations who walked at their preferred pace before rating the path difficulty (1 to 10 scale). Paths meeting the proposed accessibility guidelines were rated as either easy or moderate for difficulty of use. Slopes exceeding the guidelines may also be acceptable for very short distances or on hard/paved surfaces. Future research should include a large representative population, evaluate surface firmness, and examine different perceptions between ambulatory individuals and wheelchair users.

[7] [Wheelchair users' perceived exertion during typical mobility activities](https://consensus.app/papers/details/585093267d6d550d97506bd2d26491fa/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (L. Qi et al., 2015, 19 citations, Spinal Cord)
  Study design: Each participant performed a series of wheelchair exercises equivalent in intensity to minimal functional speed (1 m s(-1)), functional walking speed (1.3 m s(-1)), a relatively challenging speed (1.6 m s(-1)) and a self-selected speed. Each participant also completed a graded exercise test (GXT) to volitional exhaustion (VO2peak).

Objectives: The purpose of this study was (1) to assess the physical capacity of wheelchair users as they undertake typical mobility activities and (2) to investigate how closely the components of a differentiated model of perceived exertion mirror wheelchair users' own perception of exertion.

Methods: Eleven (eight males and three females) spinal cord-injured or congenitally impaired wheelchair-dependent participants volunteered for the study. Differentiated ratings of perceived exertion (RPE_arm and RPE_respiration) and oxygen uptake (VO2) and heart rate were recorded during each exercise.

Results: The mean comfortable speed at which the participants propelled their own wheelchairs on the wheelchair ergometer was 1.1±0.2 m s(-1). Speeds of 1 m s(-1) and 1.3 m s(-1) are typical of everyday functional propulsion. The corresponding RPE_respiration and RPE_arm ranged from 7 to 13 on the Borg scale; the %VO2peak measured in these trials ranged from 37 to 80% VO2peak. For propulsion intensities used in the present study-low, moderate, high and graded exercise intensity-no difference could be observed between RPE_respiration and RPE_arm. There were no significant differences between RPE_arm and RPE_respiration at the termination of the GXT.

Conclusion: The current study showed potential for the use of RPE to assess and monitor daily wheelchair propulsion intensity in individuals with paraplegia.

[8] [Accessibility of Urban Forests and Parks for People with Disabilities in Wheelchairs, Considering the Surface and Longitudinal Slope of the Trails](https://consensus.app/papers/details/e36d87386b8f588486b4359475d400b7/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (Kruno Lepoglavec et al., 2023, 21 citations, Sustainability)
  This research deals with the problem of the accessibility of urban forests and parks for people with disabilities in wheelchairs. Through an analysis of spatial data, trails were categorized on the basis of the measurements of the independent movements of eight subjects on six trails. The critical longitudinal slopes were determined for independent movement in wheelchairs, complex independent movement with certain risk, and categories of trails that are not suitable for wheelchair movement. The results indicate that a slope of 5.50% was the tipping point, after which all respondents experienced some uncertainty. In addition, a gradient of more than 9.01% was almost impassable for people in wheelchairs, with respect to the gravel trails examined in this study. Modern measurement technology was used in the field, including the mobile apps GAIA GPS and GNSS GPS, and a total (geodetic) station; the subjects’ heart rates were measured using a Garmin Fenix 6 Pro watch. In addition, people with disabilities were included in the implementation of the research through the Croatian Association of Paraplegics and Tetraplegics (HUPT). The results indicate the zones/trails that disabled people in wheelchairs can pass independently, the zones that can be accessed with a certain risk, and those that are not accessible, all according to the defined longitudinal slope zones using measurements of the movement of people in a wheelchair, their heart rate loads, and personal communication with the subjects regarding the insecurity they felt.

[9] [The Effect of External Power Output and Its Reliability on Propulsion Technique Variables in Wheelchair Users With Spinal Cord Injury](https://consensus.app/papers/details/6598ac92206355d99c9e8d797ec91245/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (S. de Groot et al., 2022, 4 citations, IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering)
  The purpose of this study was to assess 1) how treadmill slope variance affected external power output (PO) and propulsion technique reliability; and 2) how PO is associated with propulsion technique. Eighteen individuals with spinal cord injury performed two wheelchair treadmill exercise blocks (0% and 1% treadmill slope, standardized velocity) twice on two separate days. PO, velocity, and 14 propulsion technique variables were measured. In a follow-up study, N = 29 performed wheelchair treadmill drag tests. Target and actual slope were documented and PO, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and smallest detectable differences (SDD) were calculated. Within and between visits, the reliability study ICCs were perfect for velocity (1.0), weak for PO (0.33-0.46), and acceptable (>0.70) for five (0% slope) and 10 (1% slope) propulsion technique variables, resulting in SDDs of 35-196%. Measured PO explained 56-90% of the variance in key propulsion technique variables. In the follow-up, PO ICCs were weak (0.43) and SDDs high. Bias between target and actual slope appeared random. In conclusion, PO variability accounts for 50-90% of the variability in propulsion technique variables when speed and wheelchair set-up are held constant. Therefore, small differences in PO between interventions could mask the effect of the interventions on propulsion technique.

[10] [Effects of Ramp Slope and Height on Usability and Physiology during Wheelchair Driving](https://consensus.app/papers/details/62b10c8515065ea294053bc0cc2f5856/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (C. Kim et al., 2010, 8 citations, Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting)
  A ramp is the basic type of an assisting device for wheelchair users. Although the height of a ramp is an important design element, it has not been considered in prior studies. Therefore, in this study, the ramp slope and height are considered as independent variables. To analyze the effects of the slope and height, five levels of slope (1:6, 1:8, 1:10, 1:12 and 1:14) and three levels of height (15 cm, 30 cm and 45 cm) are considered. For the dependent variables, the total time and velocity were considered as performance measures, pulse rate changes and EMG signals of four related muscles (extensor carpi radialis, triceps brachii, anterior deltoid and posterior deltoid) were considered as physiology measures, and perceived discomfort while ascending and descending were considered as perceived discomfort measures. As a result, differences among performance, physiological characteristic and perceived discomfort for the five slopes increased as the height increased. Additionally, slope effects were minor when the height was low (15 cm). In summary, there was no significant difference between 1:10 and 1:12 (as suggested by ADAAG). In addition, slope effects were minor at a low height; thus, a slope of 1:8 can be recommended if the installation space for a gentler ramp is not sufficient.

IMPORTANT INSTRUCTIONS: When discussing these findings, you MUST cite papers inline using their numbered references, e.g. [1], [2]. Example: 'Caffeine improves endurance performance [1] and reduces perceived exertion [3].' Hyperlink paper titles directly: [Paper Title](url). Use the exact URLs above — do not modify or shorten them.

Participants were 23 men and women, 23 to 67 years, with vision or mobility limitations who walked at their preferred pace before rating the path difficulty (1 to 10 scale). Paths meeting the proposed accessibility guidelines were rated as either easy or moderate for difficulty of use. Slopes exceeding the guidelines may also be acceptable for very short distances or on hard/paved surfaces. Future research should include a large representative population, evaluate surface firmness, and examine different perceptions between ambulatory individuals and wheelchair users.

[7] [Wheelchair users' perceived exertion during typical mobility activities](https://consensus.app/papers/details/585093267d6d550d97506bd2d26491fa/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (L. Qi et al., 2015, 19 citations, Spinal Cord)
  Study design: Each participant performed a series of wheelchair exercises equivalent in intensity to minimal functional speed (1 m s(-1)), functional walking speed (1.3 m s(-1)), a relatively challenging speed (1.6 m s(-1)) and a self-selected speed. Each participant also completed a graded exercise test (GXT) to volitional exhaustion (VO2peak).

Objectives: The purpose of this study was (1) to assess the physical capacity of wheelchair users as they undertake typical mobility activities and (2) to investigate how closely the components of a differentiated model of perceived exertion mirror wheelchair users' own perception of exertion.

Methods: Eleven (eight males and three females) spinal cord-injured or congenitally impaired wheelchair-dependent participants volunteered for the study. Differentiated ratings of perceived exertion (RPE_arm and RPE_respiration) and oxygen uptake (VO2) and heart rate were recorded during each exercise.

Results: The mean comfortable speed at which the participants propelled their own wheelchairs on the wheelchair ergometer was 1.1±0.2 m s(-1). Speeds of 1 m s(-1) and 1.3 m s(-1) are typical of everyday functional propulsion. The corresponding RPE_respiration and RPE_arm ranged from 7 to 13 on the Borg scale; the %VO2peak measured in these trials ranged from 37 to 80% VO2peak. For propulsion intensities used in the present study-low, moderate, high and graded exercise intensity-no difference could be observed between RPE_respiration and RPE_arm. There were no significant differences between RPE_arm and RPE_respiration at the termination of the GXT.

Conclusion: The current study showed potential for the use of RPE to assess and monitor daily wheelchair propulsion intensity in individuals with paraplegia.

[8] [Accessibility of Urban Forests and Parks for People with Disabilities in Wheelchairs, Considering the Surface and Longitudinal Slope of the Trails](https://consensus.app/papers/details/e36d87386b8f588486b4359475d400b7/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (Kruno Lepoglavec et al., 2023, 21 citations, Sustainability)
  This research deals with the problem of the accessibility of urban forests and parks for people with disabilities in wheelchairs. Through an analysis of spatial data, trails were categorized on the basis of the measurements of the independent movements of eight subjects on six trails. The critical longitudinal slopes were determined for independent movement in wheelchairs, complex independent movement with certain risk, and categories of trails that are not suitable for wheelchair movement. The results indicate that a slope of 5.50% was the tipping point, after which all respondents experienced some uncertainty. In addition, a gradient of more than 9.01% was almost impassable for people in wheelchairs, with respect to the gravel trails examined in this study. Modern measurement technology was used in the field, including the mobile apps GAIA GPS and GNSS GPS, and a total (geodetic) station; the subjects’ heart rates were measured using a Garmin Fenix 6 Pro watch. In addition, people with disabilities were included in the implementation of the research through the Croatian Association of Paraplegics and Tetraplegics (HUPT). The results indicate the zones/trails that disabled people in wheelchairs can pass independently, the zones that can be accessed with a certain risk, and those that are not accessible, all according to the defined longitudinal slope zones using measurements of the movement of people in a wheelchair, their heart rate loads, and personal communication with the subjects regarding the insecurity they felt.

[9] [The Effect of External Power Output and Its Reliability on Propulsion Technique Variables in Wheelchair Users With Spinal Cord Injury](https://consensus.app/papers/details/6598ac92206355d99c9e8d797ec91245/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (S. de Groot et al., 2022, 4 citations, IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering)
  The purpose of this study was to assess 1) how treadmill slope variance affected external power output (PO) and propulsion technique reliability; and 2) how PO is associated with propulsion technique. Eighteen individuals with spinal cord injury performed two wheelchair treadmill exercise blocks (0% and 1% treadmill slope, standardized velocity) twice on two separate days. PO, velocity, and 14 propulsion technique variables were measured. In a follow-up study, N = 29 performed wheelchair treadmill drag tests. Target and actual slope were documented and PO, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and smallest detectable differences (SDD) were calculated. Within and between visits, the reliability study ICCs were perfect for velocity (1.0), weak for PO (0.33-0.46), and acceptable (>0.70) for five (0% slope) and 10 (1% slope) propulsion technique variables, resulting in SDDs of 35-196%. Measured PO explained 56-90% of the variance in key propulsion technique variables. In the follow-up, PO ICCs were weak (0.43) and SDDs high. Bias between target and actual slope appeared random. In conclusion, PO variability accounts for 50-90% of the variability in propulsion technique variables when speed and wheelchair set-up are held constant. Therefore, small differences in PO between interventions could mask the effect of the interventions on propulsion technique.

[10] [Effects of Ramp Slope and Height on Usability and Physiology during Wheelchair Driving](https://consensus.app/papers/details/62b10c8515065ea294053bc0cc2f5856/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (C. Kim et al., 2010, 8 citations, Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting)
  A ramp is the basic type of an assisting device for wheelchair users. Although the height of a ramp is an important design element, it has not been considered in prior studies. Therefore, in this study, the ramp slope and height are considered as independent variables. To analyze the effects of the slope and height, five levels of slope (1:6, 1:8, 1:10, 1:12 and 1:14) and three levels of height (15 cm, 30 cm and 45 cm) are considered. For the dependent variables, the total time and velocity were considered as performance measures, pulse rate changes and EMG signals of four related muscles (extensor carpi radialis, triceps brachii, anterior deltoid and posterior deltoid) were considered as physiology measures, and perceived discomfort while ascending and descending were considered as perceived discomfort measures. As a result, differences among performance, physiological characteristic and perceived discomfort for the five slopes increased as the height increased. Additionally, slope effects were minor when the height was low (15 cm). In summary, there was no significant difference between 1:10 and 1:12 (as suggested by ADAAG). In addition, slope effects were minor at a low height; thus, a slope of 1:8 can be recommended if the installation space for a gentler ramp is not sufficient.

entries.description:
Search over 220 million peer-reviewed academic papers.

Use this tool when the user asks about research, studies, evidence,
scientific findings, clinical trials, medical research, or academic
literature. Covers Semantic Scholar, PubMed, Scopus, and ArXiv.

Returns paper titles, authors, abstracts, citation counts, journal
quality scores, and direct URLs to each paper.
All filters are optional — only apply them when the user explicitly asks.

Example query → filter mappings:
- "what does the evidence say about metformin for longevity?"
    → query="metformin longevity mortality",
      medical_mode=True, exclude_preprints=True
- "recent peer-reviewed RCTs on SGLT2 inhibitors for heart failure"
    → query="SGLT2 inhibitors heart failure outcomes",
      year_min=2022, exclude_preprints=True, study_types=["rct"]
- "long-term studies of statin side effects (1+ year)"
    → query="statin adverse effects long-term",
      duration_min=365, medical_mode=True
- "what is dark matter?"
    → query="dark matter"  (no filters — general question)
- "coffee and cognition, excluding top-tier Q1 journals"
    → query="coffee cognition", sjr_min=2

query.description: Search query. Be specific and use academic terminology.

year_min.description: Minimum publication year. Set ONLY when the user asks for recent / latest / 'in the last N years' research. Do NOT set by default.

year_max.description: Maximum publication year. Set ONLY when the user asks for historical research before a specific date. Rarely set.

month_min.description: Minimum publication month, paired with year_min. Set ONLY when the user specifies a lower-bound month or exact date such as 'after March 2020'. Do NOT set without year_min.

month_max.description: Maximum publication month, paired with year_max. Set ONLY when the user specifies an upper-bound month or exact date such as 'through June 2022'. Do NOT set without year_max.

human.description: Restrict to human studies only. Set ONLY when the user explicitly asks for human / clinical / patient studies (or to exclude animal / in-vitro work). Do NOT set by default for medical, health, or clinical questions — the corpus already includes the relevant human evidence and filtering here may exclude valuable translational, mechanism, or preclinical context.

controlled.description: Restrict to controlled studies. Set ONLY when the user explicitly asks for controlled studies or controlled trials. Do NOT set by default.

sample_size_min.description: Minimum participant count. Set ONLY when the user asks for large or well-powered studies. Do NOT set by default — many high-quality studies are small by design.

citation_min.description: Minimum citation count. Set ONLY when the user explicitly asks for highly-cited or influential work. Do NOT infer from words like 'seminal' or 'foundational'. Do NOT set by default.

study_types.description: Filter by study design. Set ONLY when the user names a design ('RCT', 'meta-analysis', 'systematic review') or asks for 'best' / 'highest-quality' / 'rigorous' evidence (then use ['rct', 'meta-analysis', 'systematic review']). Do NOT set for general research questions — narrowing by design excludes valid evidence.

domain.description: Comma-separated academic field short codes, not email or web domains. Set ONLY when the user explicitly asks to limit results to specific academic disciplines or fields. Valid codes: med, bio, cs, chem, psych, phys, mat, eng, env, bus, econ, math, poli, agri, edu, soc, geol, geog, hist, art, philo, law, ling. Examples: 'medical papers' -> 'med', 'biology and computer science' -> 'bio,cs'. Do NOT set for general research questions.

sjr_max.description: Maximum journal ranking quartile (1=Q1 top → 4=Q4). Set ONLY when the user explicitly asks for top-tier / Q1 / high-impact-journal results. Do NOT set by default — many landmark and niche-field studies publish outside Q1.

sjr_min.description: Minimum journal-ranking quartile floor (1=Q1 top -> 4=Q4). Keeps journals at or below this quartile rank, i.e. it EXCLUDES the very top tiers. Set ONLY when the user explicitly asks to exclude top-tier / Q1 journals. For 'top-tier / Q1 / high-impact', use sjr_max instead, never sjr_min. Rarely set.

medical_mode.description: Filter to top medical journals and clinical guidelines (~8M documents). Set to true for clinical / medical / evidence-based-medicine questions (e.g. drug efficacy, treatment comparisons, diagnostic criteria, NEJM/JAMA/Lancet-tier evidence requests). Pairs well with exclude_preprints=true.

exclude_preprints.description: True to exclude preprints and return peer-reviewed papers only. Set when the user asks for 'peer-reviewed', 'published', 'vetted' research or explicitly 'no preprints'.

open_access.description: Restrict to open-access papers. Set ONLY when the user explicitly asks for open-access or free-to-read papers. Do NOT set by default. Note: 'open source' is NOT 'open access'.

duration_min.description: Minimum study duration in DAYS. Set when the user asks for longitudinal / long-term / multi-year studies. Typical thresholds: 30 (month), 365 (year), 730 (2+ years).

duration_max.description: Maximum study duration in DAYS. Rarely set.

publisher_name.description: Comma-separated publisher display names to filter by. Set ONLY when the user explicitly asks for papers from a specific publisher (e.g. 'Elsevier', 'Nature', 'PLOS ONE'). Do NOT set by default.

journal_name.description: Preferred journal name (e.g. 'Nature'). Results from matching journals are surfaced higher; this does not exclude other journals. Set ONLY when the user explicitly asks to prefer a specific journal. Do NOT set by default.

country.description: Comma-separated ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes (e.g. 'us', 'gb') to limit to those countries of study. Set ONLY when the user explicitly names a country or region of study. Do NOT infer from the query's language or topic. Unknown codes are ignored.

page.description: Zero-indexed result page. Set ONLY when the user explicitly asks for more or next results. Pages above 0 are available with paid plans (Pro, Deep, Teams, Enterprise) or an Enterprise API key.

page_size.description: Number of results to return per page. Set ONLY when the user explicitly asks for a specific page size. If omitted, the caller's tier default is used.

include_full_text_chunks.description: Return query-relevant full-text excerpts. Set ONLY when the user explicitly asks for excerpts from full text and has a paid plan (Pro, Deep, Teams, Enterprise).

entries.name: mcp__Scholar_Gateway__semanticSearch
entries.description: Searches a full-text academic corpus and returns relevant passages with citation metadata. Use for research questions, factual claims, literature-backed explanations, evidence-based summaries, and in any responses where academic support would improve accuracy, credibility, or depth. Submit queries as complete natural language questions, preserving the full intent — do not reduce to keywords. For ambiguous or polysemous terms, always expand to their full context before searching: use "multiple sclerosis" not "MS", "Java programming language" not "Java". Prefer precise scientific or clinical terminology over colloquial terms: use "rhinovirus upper respiratory tract infection" rather than "common cold". Cite all substantive claims inline using author-year format with DOI hyperlinks. If no results are returned, broaden the query or try an alternative framing — do not retry the same query.

query.description: Natural language research question. Preserve intent, scope, and structure. Rewrite for semantic clarity but do not compress to keywords. Expand acronyms and add field context for ambiguous or polysemous terms.

topN.description: Number of passages to return. Higher values improve recall for broad or multi-faceted queries; lower values are appropriate for narrow or well-defined topics.

start_year.description: Inclusive lower bound for publication year filter. Omit to search across all available years.

end_year.description: Inclusive upper bound for publication year filter. Omit to include publications up to the present.

includeRetractedContent.description: Whether to include retracted publications in results. Default false; set true only when retraction history is itself the subject of inquiry.

I found information about wheelchair ramp accessibility standards. Here are the key findings:

## Wheelchair Ramp Gradient Standards

**ADA Standards (USA):**
The ADA requires that all business and public use wheelchair ramps adhere to a 1:12 slope ratio, meaning that for every inch of vertical rise there must be 12 horizontal inches (one foot) of ramp. For residential ramp applications, it is suggested that residential ramps adhere to a standard with a slope up to (but not more than) a 2:12 ratio, or one foot of ramp for every 2 inches of vertical rise.

**Alternative Standards (UK):**
The recommended maximum gradient is 1:15 (4 degrees) and the preferred maximum gradient is 1:20 (3 degrees). A ramp at 1:15 should not exceed 10m without a resting platform, while a ramp at 1:20 should not exceed 30m without a resting platform.

## Other Key Ramp Requirements

Ramps must be at least 36 inches wide to accommodate mobility devices comfortably and guarantee easy passage for individuals using wheelchairs or walkers. Regular audits can help ensure ramps remain safe, slip-resistant, and code-compliant.

cand () { GUIDEBOOK_DB_PATH="$G" python3 scripts/db.py add-candidate --session "$SESS" --found-under-slug accessible-circulation-geometry "$@"; }

cand --exec-id 71 --disposition PENDING-VERIFICATION --tier-guess 1 \
 --title 'Impact of Running Slope and Cross Slope on the Difficulty Level of Outdoor Pathways (Longmuir, Environment and Behavior, 2003)' \
 --locator 'surfaced via Consensus; DOI not yet resolved' --locator-status UNVERIFIED \
 --why-not-admitted 'HYPOTHESIS, AND THE HIGHEST-VALUE LEAD OF THIS BATCH. A SECOND independent perceived-difficulty study on running slope AND cross slope -- 23 participants with vision or mobility limitations rating path difficulty against PROPOSED accessibility guidelines. That is GAP-002 acceptability question directly, from a different laboratory and six years before REF-01002. Its reported finding that slopes exceeding the guidelines may also be acceptable FOR VERY SHORT DISTANCES or on hard/paved surfaces is DISTANCE-CONDITIONED in the same way REF-01002 7 percent is conditioned on 20 ft and REF-00996 states as its mechanism -- three sources, three methods, one conditioning structure. NOT ADMITTED: reached through a Consensus record, not a retrieved payload; needs the R10 ladder and a tier call. Note the population is mixed vision AND mobility, so the match grade will not be EXACT.'

cand --exec-id 71 --disposition PENDING-VERIFICATION --tier-guess 1 \
 --title 'Effects of Ramp Slope and Height on Usability and Physiology during Wheelchair Driving (Kim et al., HFES Proceedings, 2010)' \
 --locator 'surfaced via Consensus; DOI not yet resolved' --locator-status UNVERIFIED \
 --why-not-admitted 'HYPOTHESIS. Five slope levels (1:6, 1:8, 1:10, 1:12, 1:14) crossed with THREE RISE HEIGHTS (15, 30, 45 cm) -- the rise-conditioned design this parameter needs and has never had in the corpus, plus perceived discomfort alongside EMG and pulse. Its reported conclusions bear directly on two live questions: no significant difference between 1:10 and 1:12, and slope effects minor at low rise. RELATED TO BUT NOT THE SAME AS candidate 88 (Kim 2014), which GAP-008 blocked -- this is the 2010 HFES paper, and the pair should be resolved together. Not admitted: Consensus record, not a retrieved payload.'

cand --exec-id 74 --disposition PENDING-VERIFICATION --tier-guess 3 \
 --title 'Four architectural movement studies for the wheelchair and ambulant disabled. Part 3 - Ramp gradients (1971)' \
 --locator 'no DOI; entry 24 of 25 in REF-00980 Crossref deposit' --locator-status UNVERIFIED \
 --why-not-admitted 'HYPOTHESIS, AND POSSIBLY THE ROOT OF THE 1:12 LINEAGE. A 1971 architectural movement study whose Part 3 is titled Ramp gradients, cited by the 1997 study that tested the ADA-permitted range. If the modern codes trace to a measurement study, this is a strong candidate for where. NO DOI, so unreachable by every DOI-keyed method this project runs -- resolution needs a library or archive route, which is a different kind of work from a Crossref chase and should be planned as such rather than attempted opportunistically.'

cand --exec-id 74 --disposition PENDING-VERIFICATION --tier-guess 3 \
 --title 'A study to determine the specifications of wheelchair ramps (1957)' \
 --locator 'no DOI; entry 9 of 25 in REF-00980 Crossref deposit' --locator-status UNVERIFIED \
 --why-not-admitted 'HYPOTHESIS. The oldest ramp-specification study in any reference list this corpus holds. Same locator problem as the 1971 study and the same reason to want it: a specification study from 1957 is either the origin of a threshold still in force or evidence that the threshold was never measured at all, and both answers matter to GAP-002.'

cand --exec-id 74 --disposition PENDING-VERIFICATION --tier-guess 3 \
 --title 'Accessibility by means of ramps - Some research data from the Netherlands (1981)' \
 --locator 'no DOI; entry 22 of 25 in REF-00980 Crossref deposit' --locator-status UNVERIFIED \
 --why-not-admitted 'HYPOTHESIS. Non-English-origin empirical ramp research, and R5 applies: non-indexation is an INDEXING fact, not an evidence-quality fact. The corpus already holds REF-00996, a Flemish handbook stating the rise-conditioning mechanism; a 1981 Dutch research paper may be part of the same lineage and would be a second non-anglophone empirical input on this parameter.'

cand --exec-id 73 --disposition PENDING-VERIFICATION --tier-guess 1 \
 --title 'A kinetic analysis of manual wheelchair propulsion during start-up on select indoor and outdoor surfaces (JRRD, 2005)' \
 --locator '10.1682/JRRD.2004.08.0106' --locator-status UNVERIFIED \
 --why-not-admitted 'HYPOTHESIS. JRRD, therefore open access and cheaply retrievable. Start-up kinetics across surfaces rather than a slope series, so it likely bears on surface rather than gradient -- staged for completeness of the M2 seam and ranked below the slope-series papers.'

cand --exec-id 73 --disposition PENDING-VERIFICATION --tier-guess 3 \
 --title 'An evaluation of portable ramps (British Journal of Occupational Therapy, 1989)' \
 --locator '10.1177/030802268905201209' --locator-status UNVERIFIED \
 --why-not-admitted 'HYPOTHESIS, AND A CROSS-CONFIRMATION WORTH NAMING. A second 1989 portable-ramp paper, sitting beside 10.3109/03790798909166390 which batch 16 already staged as candidate 101 from a DIFFERENT anchor. Two anchors reference sets overlapping exactly where the GAP-018 predictor says they should is weak independent support for the predictor. British Journal of Occupational Therapy is an OT professional venue, so the Co-2 question applies on retrieval.'
echo "=== candidates staged ==="
